title: Last Year's Profit Sets the Floor. Your Growth Story Sets the Multiple.
linkedin:
Two businesses in the same industry, with near identical profit, can sell for very different prices. One goes for three times profit. The other goes for six.

The gap almost never sits in the numbers a buyer already has. It sits in the numbers they don't have yet, the twelve to twenty four months after settlement.

A buyer isn't really paying for what a business earned last year. They're paying for what they believe it will earn once they own it, discounted for the risk that belief turns out wrong.

That's why "we're growing" convinces almost no one on its own. Buyers have heard that from every vendor they've sat across from.

What actually moves a buyer is evidence they can check themselves. The proportion of revenue that's contracted or recurring rather than one off. Retention and renewal figures tracked over several years, not one good quarter. A documented pipeline with a real conversion history. Forecasts that were actually hit in the past two or three years, not quietly revised down each time.

There's a second layer too. If the pipeline is full because the owner has spent fifteen years building the right relationships personally, a buyer discounts it, because there's no guarantee it survives a change of ownership.

None of this gets built in the weeks before a business goes to market. It's the output of two or three years of consistent forecasting discipline, tracked and proven.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

Here's something we see a lot with business owners thinking about an eventual sale: two businesses with almost identical profit can end up selling for very different prices.

The difference usually isn't in last year's numbers. It's whether a buyer actually believes what happens next, and whether there's real evidence behind that belief rather than just an owner's confidence.

Genuine question for anyone who's sold, or thought about it: when you picture your business changing hands, how much of the future pipeline runs through relationships only you hold?

That one's worth sitting with.

A note for East Coast business owners who have ever wondered what actually decides the price a business sells for. It isn't only last year's profit.

Two businesses in the same industry, with near identical profit, can sell for very different multiples. Buyers are paying for what they believe the business will earn after settlement, not what it earned before it. That belief has to be backed by evidence, not just an owner's confidence that things are heading in the right direction.

The businesses that sell well tend to have a few things in common. A meaningful share of contracted or recurring revenue. Renewal and retention figures tracked over several years rather than one good quarter. A documented pipeline with a real conversion history behind it. And a track record of hitting forecasts, rather than quietly revising them down.

None of that gets built in the final few months before a sale. It's usually two or three years of consistent forecasting discipline, and it tends to make for a better run business along the way too, whether or not a sale is on the horizon.
